power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introducing Tremor Morphology Toolkit (TMT), an eight-metric framework for objective tremor characterization.

Correlation analysis identified redundant and complementary relationships among tremor-shape features, with sinusoidal waveform characteristics (rSINE), cycle-to-cycle amplitude variability (rCVA), and tremor frequency variability (FreqVar) providing a concise, complementary set for characterizing tremor shape.

Examination of the alignment between newly defined tremor-shape features and clinician perceptions found that clinicians relied more on envelope-based amplitude dynamics than on individual tremor cycles.

"Tremor" is often used as an umbrella term for repetitive movements with multiple subtypes, each with distinct pathophysiology making precise characterization crucial for diagnosis and treatment.
It is defined as an involuntary, oscillatory, repetitive back-and-forth movement of a body part about a fixed point, axis, or plane (Crawford and Zimmerman, 2018; Shaikh et al., 2024)).
text.formatted: It is defined as an involuntary, oscillatory, repetitive back-and-forth movement of a body part about a fixed point, axis, or plane <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford and Zimmerman, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Shaikh et al., 2024)</ref>).

text.text: Traditionally, tremor is described by its frequency, amplitude, distribution (location, symmetry and laterality), and activation (rest vs action) (Albanese and Sorbo, 2016; Algarni and Fasano, 2018; Alty and Kempster, 2011; Stouwe et al., 2020; Thenganatt and Jankovic, 2016).

text.text: Beyond rate and magnitude, the trajectory shape i.e. morphology of the movement can provide additional diagnostic cues.
Clinicians visually assess whether the path is regular or jerky and how consistent that pattern remains over time.
Qualitative descriptors that complement these metrics include amplitude variability, frequency variability, the shape of the movement trajectory, the consistency of that shape over time.
Several of these features can be subtle or require extensive expertise to detect, allowing subjective weighting of parameters to influence the assessment.
Such limitations contribute to frequent misdiagnosis, delaying optimal therapy (Rizzo et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Such limitations contribute to frequent misdiagnosis, delaying optimal therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Rizzo et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Imaging and deep brain stimulation studies link essential tremor-like head oscillations to cerebellar circuits projecting via the ventral intermediate (VIM) thalamus and dentatothalamic tracts, which clinically manifest as regular, rhythmic cycles (Erro et al., 2022; Panyakaew et al., 2022).

text.text: In contrast, oscillations co-occurring with dystonia are characterized by impaired inhibition at multiple levels and pallidal unit activity with burst-pause patterns, yielding irregular, "saw-tooth" kinematics and frequent antagonist co-contraction or overflow on EMG (Ulia Semenova et al., 2021).

text.text: Consistent with these clinicalphysiological distinctions, spectral measures such as half-power bandwidth (Murgai and Iskhakova, 2025) and the Tremor Stability Index (Biase et al., 2017) tend to broaden and destabilize with jerky morphology, aiding discrimination of dystonia when present with tremor from the more regular ET-like pattern.

text.text: Hence, metrics that address waveform shape and its variance over time are needed to complement frequency and amplitude, capturing regularity, cycle morphology, and modulation stability that map onto underlying circuit contributions.
Traditional tremor characterization has primarily emphasized the body distribution of tremor, along with its amplitude and frequency.

Clinical rating scales such as the Tremor Research Group Essential Tremor Rating Assessment Scale (TETRAS) similarly place substantial emphasis on tremor amplitude across different body regions and tasks (Elble, 2016).

text.text: However, tremors with similar amplitudes or dominant frequencies may differ in their waveform structure and temporal behavior, suggesting that additional characteristics including waveform shape, amplitude dynamics, and cycle-to-cycle frequency stability may provide complementary information about tremor phenomenology.
The definitions of these features can be subjective and prone to varying interpretations.

Our interrater reliability study using a basic trajectory shape revealed markedly lower agreement for tremor morphology than for broader characteristics such as presence, symmetry, and frequency, underscoring the need for an objective, standardized framework (Joshi et al., 2026).

Whether these discrepancies reflect true physiology or clinician bias, they motivate methods that (i) disentangle frequency modulation from amplitude-based modulation and (ii) isolate amplitude effects from waveform shape.

We therefore introduce the Tremor Morphology Toolkit (TMT) with eight features, an objective framework that independently quantifies amplitude variability, frequency variability, waveformshape consistency, and sinusoidal nature (how closely the average cycle of tremor approximates a sine wave) from inertial-measurement-unit accelerometer and gyroscope data suited to the non-stationary nature of tremor signals.
This study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the University of Toronto Institutional Review Board.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.
Data were collected from 34 participants with clinically diagnosed upper-limb tremor.
Based on clinical assessment, participants were categorized as having essential tremor (n = 16), Parkinsonian tremor (n = 6), dystonic tremor (n = 4), or other tremor (n = 8).

Tremor was assessed during standard positions and tasks, including rest (arms resting on the armchair), postural tremor (arms extended at shoulder height), wing tremor (forearms folded toward the chest with elbows lifted outward), and kinetic tremor (index-to-nose maneuver).
Tremor recordings were obtained using an Xsens DOT inertial measurement unit (IMU; Movella Inc., Enschede, The Netherlands) secured to the participant's palm with an adjustable strap.
Data were sampled at 60 Hz for a minimum of 30 s per trial.
Each recording was stored in .xlsx format for subsequent analysis.

A videotape was also obtained as the participants performed the tasks and subsequently rated by four movement disorder for use under a CC0 license. neurologists using the Tremor Waveform Morphology Questionnaire (Joshi et al., 2026).

Each new cycle therefore begins at every other zerocrossing.

The first six indices were derived by summarizing features extracted from individual cycles: Amplitude Modulation Index, Frequency Modulation index, Sinusoidality Index, Shape Similarity Index, Amplitude Warping Index, and Cycle Duration warping index.

The last one is a set of amplitude breathing indices which attempt to quantify the waxing and waning patterns of amplitude change in an oscillatory tremor like movement.
Amplitude Modulation Index (rCVA): For each cycle, the peak-to-peak amplitude was computed as the difference between the maximum and minimum values.

We use a robust statistic because cycle amplitudes in tremor data are may not be Gaussian: motion artifacts, brief co-contractions, sensor clipping, and missed segments can produce outliers, skew, and heavy tails.
The standard CV (standard deviation/mean) is highly sensitive to such extremes and can overstate variability.

text.text: Following prior approaches (reference pending), rater perceptions of tremor presence, amplitude stability (constant or varying), rhythm regularity (regular or irregular), jerkiness (present or absent), and frequency range were modeled using newly defined features in the Tremor Morphology Toolkit.
We examined how objectively quantified tremor features correspond to clinicians' categorical ratings using a supervised learning framework.

Each trial (participant × arm position: rest, wing, or kinetic) was represented by eight features: rCVA, rSINE, FreqVar, peakF, peakAmp, TEBR, TEMR, and ApEn. peakAmp and peakF are the peak amplitude and the corresponding frequency of the power spectral density curve of the oscillatory component.
Trials lacking rater annotations were excluded, and when multiple raters were available, feature rows were replicated to align with individual ratings.

For each rating type (tremor presence, amplitude constancy, rhythm, jerkiness, and frequency range), features were z-scored and evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation with 10 repetitions, in which each fold comprised stratified training (80%) and test (20%) subsets to preserve class balance.

A bagged decision-tree ensemble (fitcensemble; 200 trees; minimum leaf size = 10) was trained on the training data, and model performance on the held-out test set was summarized using accuracy and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).

text.text: Although amplitude and frequency are commonly used quantitative descriptors, they may not fully capture tremor morphology and temporal variability.

The goal of this study was to establish a set of objective, intuitive, and easily interpretable metrics for quantifying tremor morphology in a feature space that reflects waveform shape, amplitude stability, and frequency regularity.

Unlike prior qualitative classifications, the features defined here: rSINE, rSHAPE, rCVA, rCVD, FreqVar, warping indices (AWI, DWI) and Amplitude Breathing Indices provide simple numerical measures that can be consistently applied across recordings and observers.
Each captures a physiologically meaningful aspect of tremor dynamics, ranging from shape regularity and cycle symmetry to amplitude and frequency stability.
Although developed here for upper-extremity tremor, the framework is readily extensible to other repetitive movements (e.g., head tremor, nystagmus, stereotypies).
The features rCVD and FreqVar were only weakly correlated.

Although both relate to frequency stability, they capture different constructs: rCVD is a time-domain, cycle-to-cycle measure of period jitter that is agnostic to spectral power, whereas FreqVar is a frequency-domain bandwidth that implicitly weights variability by how power is distributed around the peak.
Thus, rCVD can be viewed as a "pure" timing-variability metric, while FreqVar reflects a powerweighted frequency spread.
Interestingly, rCVD and rSINE were inversely related, indicating that cycle duration changes primarily occur when the waveform deviates from a perfect sinusoid.
In other words, loss of sinusoidality accompanies timing irregularity-a plausible reflection of distorted oscillatory drive or competing generators.
In our dataset, rSINE and rSHAPE are highly correlated.

Repetitive oscillations emerge when a phase-locked motor generator in the brain produces a phase-locked movement pattern.
This generator may comprise a single loop or multiple interacting oscillatory loops, so cycle-to-cycle changes can reflect their interplay.

While neuroimaging and electrophysiology aim to identify these loops, clinical assessment of the resulting symptoms is often limited to qualitative ratings or simple quantitative measures (amplitude, frequency) that may miss key dynamics.
Functionally, if a motor circuit is locked into one dominant loop, that loop should be the therapeutic target; if the circuit switches between loops, interventions should vary accordingly.

The Breath Modulation Ratio captures the strength (effective gain) of this slower modulation on the oscillation-generating circuitry.
The alignment of clinician perceptions with the newly defined features in the Tremor Morphology Toolkit revealed several notable insights.

Amplitude breathing indices had a strong influence on clinicians' perception of tremor shape, underscoring the complexity of human interpretation and the potential disconnect between descriptive language and the underlying signal dynamics.
The model for amplitude stability, despite incorporating these newly defined features, showed poor predictive performance, suggesting inconsistency in how raters perceived and defined this attribute.
This highlights a broader ambiguity in the subjective interpretation of amplitude variability across clinicians.
The model's performance may be attributed to two factors.
One possibility is that rater perception is inherently more complex than what the current feature set can capture.

A more likely explanation is that attributes such as amplitude, jerkiness, and rhythm are interpreted through individualized perceptual heuristics, with each clinician applying unique internal criteria.
In contrast, binary judgments such as the presence or absence of tremor show higher perceptual agreement, leading to better model performance.

Interestingly, across several perceptual domains-tremor presence, rhythm regularity, and jerkiness-two of the three most influential predictors were derived from envelope-based features rather than cycle-to-cycle for use under a CC0 license. measures, suggesting that clinicians may rely more on slow amplitude modulations in the envelope than on fine-grained waveform shape variations when forming perceptual judgments.
Frequency classification exhibited good overall accuracy but limited discriminative ability, likely reflecting label imbalance and perceptual ambiguity.
The "mid" frequency category was used more frequently by raters, which may have inflated overall accuracy without improving true discriminative power.
Furthermore, the absence of clearly defined perceptual boundaries between frequency groups may have introduced uncertainty into the ground truth labels, thereby reducing the model's AUC performance.

text.text: While promising, these approaches have two key limitations.
First, the "ground truth" is typically defined by clinicians and can therefore be subjective.
Second, the derived features are often opaque, reducing clinical interpretability and relevance.
These issues highlight the need for intuitive, physically, and physiologically meaningful parameters that will be used in the clinic, as well as research.
Altogether, these metrics offer a descriptive, mechanistically grounded framework for tremor characterization from as little as 30 seconds of data.

They bridge qualitative descriptions with quantitative measures that are physiologically interpretable, reproducible, and suitable for crosssubject comparisons, thereby enhancing their translational utility.
We encourage researchers to adapt and apply these parameters in conjunction with electrophysiological data to uncover shared mechanisms underlying tremor generation and modulation.

Together, such integrative analyses can advance the development of objective, interpretable biomarkers that link behavior to underlying neural dynamics, paving the way for more precise, physiology-informed therapeutic strategies.

Frequency variability (FreqVar): We estimated frequency variability (FreqVar) as the bandwidth of the central 66% of spectral energy.

For each signal, a continuous wavelet transform (32 voices/octave) was computed; time-frequency power was averaged over time to obtain a mean spectrum, normalized, and its cumulative distribution used to locate the 17th and 83rd percentiles.

Amplitude Breathing Indices (ApEn, Tremor Envelope Breathing Rate, Tremor Envelope Modulation Ratio): We quantified "breathing-like" amplitude modulations in the oscillatory component to capture slow waxing-waning of tremor amplitude.

These envelope features probe non-stationarity and organization of the signal: (i) the Tremor Envelope Breathing Rate (TEBR) (peaks of the smoothed amplitude envelope per second) indexes how often slow amplitude swells occur; (ii) the Tremor Envelope Modulation Ratio (median peak-to-trough amplitude) summarizes the strength of each swell; and (iii) approximate entropy to measure the unpredictability of these modulations.
We quantified these slow "breathing-like" amplitude modulations of the oscillatory component as follows.

Upper and lower envelopes were obtained with MATLAB's peak-based envelope function at two scales: First, a short window (1 sample) was used to calculate the upper and lower envelopes (dark red lines in Figure3plots).
Instantaneous amplitudes were computed as the difference between upper and lower envelopes.
This amplitude series was used to compute approximate entropy (ApEn) as a measure of regularity (lower ApEn = more stereotyped modulation, higher ApEn = more erratic changes).
A second envelope was calculated using a larger window (30 samples or half the sampling rate) to capture slower modulations (dark blue line in figure3plots).
